o: Recognise star and mesh network topologies.
Explain advantages and limitations of each.
Choose a suitable topology and justify why.
c: A network topology shows how computers and connection devices link together.
Each endpoint connects to a central device such as a switch. Easier to add/manage devices, but the central device is a point of failure.
Devices can connect to multiple others. Alternative paths make the system resilient if one link fails, but more connections increase cost and complexity.
For a small school LAN, a star can be practical. A high-availability network may use mesh routes; explain what happens when a link or central device fails.

m.title: School network failure
m.q: A school LAN uses a star topology. Explain one advantage and one disadvantage if its central switch fails. [4 marks]
st: All classroom devices connect to one central switch.
New devices can be connected easily [1], making the network straightforward to manage [1].
The switch is a single point of failure [1], so its failure can interrupt communication for connected devices [1].
Give advantage plus linked benefit and disadvantage plus linked effect.

w: A business needs reliable connections between several sites. Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of a mesh topology. [4 marks]
Multiple possible routes [1] mean traffic can use another path if a link fails [1]. More connections/hardware are needed [1], increasing cost or maintenance [1].
A small primary school chooses a star topology. Explain two advantages of this decision. [4 marks]
Each device has its own link to the central device [1], making fault isolation easier [1]. Devices can be added or managed centrally [1], simplifying expansion [1].
Describe how a mesh can continue operating after one connection fails. [4 marks]
Mesh provides multiple paths between devices [1]. When a link fails [1], traffic may be routed along another available path [1], keeping communication possible [1].
wSteps: Look for reliability requirement and its trade-off.
Mesh has alternative paths [1], but also requires more links [1].
Rerouting improves fault tolerance [1] while extra links cost more [1].
Multiple possible routes [1] mean traffic can use another path if a link fails [1]. More connections/hardware are needed [1], increasing cost or maintenance [1].
Dedicated links [1]; connections are managed from the central switch [1].
A single endpoint fault can be isolated [1]; adding devices is straightforward [1].
Each device has its own link to the central device [1], making fault isolation easier [1]. Devices can be added or managed centrally [1], simplifying expansion [1].
Follow the data from the failed link to another route.
Mesh has redundant connections [1]; one link stops working [1].
A different path may carry data [1], avoiding total loss of service [1].
Mesh provides multiple paths between devices [1]. When a link fails [1], traffic may be routed along another available path [1], keeping communication possible [1].

k.q: Calculate how many direct links a fully connected mesh needs for a small number of devices. This extends the topology comparison.
p: Add print("Links counted") after displaying the value.
k.a:
Four devices: 4 × 3 ÷ 2 = 6 links. Five devices: 5 × 4 ÷ 2 = 10 links.

Extended OCR ERL:
devices = 5
links = devices * (devices - 1) / 2
print(links)
print("Links counted")

Outputs: 10 and Links counted. Mathematical enrichment; OCR J277 focuses on comparing topologies.

A cinema uses a star network to connect ticket kiosks and staff computers. The central switch stops working. Explain the effect and suggest one precaution. [4 marks]

Source: Original J277-style question, not an OCR past-paper original.

The central switch connects the kiosks/computers [1], so its failure can interrupt network communication [1]. A spare or quickly replaceable switch, or a resilient design, can reduce the problem [1] by restoring service/reducing downtime [1].

Compare star and mesh topologies for a large organisation. [6 marks]

Source: Original J277-style question, not an OCR past-paper original.

Star devices connect to a central switch [1], are easier/cheaper to manage [1], but depend on the central device [1]. Mesh provides more than one path [1], so it can withstand some link failures [1], but uses extra connections increasing cost/complexity [1].
v: Arrangement of network devices and links.
Endpoints connect to a central switch or hub.
Devices connect via multiple paths between nodes.
Ability to continue working after some faults.
Network device that connects and forwards data to LAN devices.
Extra paths that can be used if a path fails.
x: Mesh topology generally provides alternative links that can improve fault tolerance.
